findings.location: §5A ("The enforcers") and the census table in §6A; secondary mention in §7A
findings.issue: ELSPR (arXiv:2505.17691, AAAI 2026) is a fully implemented, published TRAINING-TIME repair intervention on preference data that the report never mentions in any form. It models pairwise preference data as a tournament graph, quantifies non-transitivity via strongly-connected-component analysis and a normalized directed-graph structural-entropy metric, and selectively DELETES the preference pairs that induce non-transitivity while preserving the transitive ones. This is exactly the Grade III / data-pipeline-filter category the report defines in §1A and assigns to GARP-EFM's rejection sampling [5] — and it is arc-deletion on a revealed-preference graph, i.e. the machine-learning-side rediscovery of the Dean-Martin minimum-cost-index construction the report discusses at §2B and §8B. Its omission understates the census count, leaves §8B's "cycle deletion" rediscovery paragraph without its strongest ML-side instance, and drops a downstream data point.
findings.evidence: Vault note `250517691-elspr-evaluator-llm-training-data-self-purification-on-non-transitive` (tagged to this run, status evergreen). Abstract: "ELSPR, a principled graph-theoretic framework that models pairwise preferences as tournament graphs and systematically identifies problematic training data... quantifies non-transitivity through strongly connected components (SCCs) analysis and measures overall preference clarity using a novel normalized directed graph structural entropy metric. Our filtering methodology selectively removes preference data that induce non-transitivity while preserving transitive preferences." Reported results on AlpacaEval: "a 13.8% reduction in non-transitivity, a 0.088 decrease in structural entropy, and significantly enhanced discriminative power"; human validation: discarded data show inter-annotator agreement 34.4% vs 52.6% and model-human consistency 51.2% vs 80.6% relative to retained data. The report's own grep surface is empty for "ELSPR", "self-purification", "structural entropy" and "AlpacaEval".
findings.recommendation: Add ELSPR as a named enforcer in §5A (a short paragraph in the same register as the isotonic-score-repair and dual-track paragraphs), and add it as a new row in the §6A census table: Front=ML, Timing=Training, Axiom=transitivity (tournament acyclicity), Formally minimal?=No (heuristic SCC-based deletion, not a minimum-cost solution), Downstream metric=judge discriminative power plus human inter-annotator agreement, Exogenous?=Partly, Sign=Positive. The counts in the paragraph directly under the table ("Twelve entries... Seven act at inference time and five at training time") must be updated. Also add one clause to §8B's "Cycle deletion" paragraph noting that ELSPR performs precisely the arc-deletion-on-a-preference-graph operation the economics side proved NP-hard, again without citing that literature.

findings.location: §5A / §6A census row 10 / §7 (the empirical record on coherence vs. downstream quality)
findings.issue: The corpus contains a dual-timing (inference-time AND training-time) probabilistic-coherence intervention with an explicit downstream-accuracy result, and the report omits it. Worse, census row 10 lists "Coherence-targeted fine-tuning on probabilistic axioms [7] ... de Finetti coherence; martingale consistency ... Positive where reported" while §3B and the exclusion list in §6A both state that [7] is specified but NEVER RUN ("No model is trained in it"). Row 10 is therefore either miscited or unsupported, and the actual martingale-coherence intervention that would support it sits uncited in the vault. This omission also removes the only clean NULL result from §7: the report currently presents positives and three failures but no case of "coherence up, task quality unchanged," which is a distinct and important third direction for a question that explicitly asks about the relationship "in either direction."
findings.evidence: Vault note `260617832-from-drift-to-coherence-stabilizing-beliefs-in-llms` (arXiv:2606.17832), tagged `training-time-intervention`, `inference-time-intervention`, `probabilistic-coherence`, `martingale-property`, `downstream-eval`. Extracted claim (research/temp/claims-260617832-...json): "we further propose (i) a seed-answer prompting strategy to accelerate stabilization, and (ii) a self-consistency loss that amortizes early-stage drift into the model via fine-tuning. Experiments on multiple-choice QA benchmarks show that our methods substantially reduce belief drift and improve predictive coherence without sacrificing accuracy." Related uncited note `251225070-scaling-open-ended-reasoning-to-predict-the-future` (OpenForecaster-8B): RL fine-tuning "improves the accuracy, calibration, AND consistency of predictions," with calibration gains generalizing across benchmarks — a second instance of coherence and quality moving together, and direct evidence bearing on §7C's own falsifiable prediction that an information-ADDING coherence operator should improve coherence and accuracy together. Report grep: "drift" 0 hits, "seed-answer" 0 hits, "OpenForecaster" 0 hits; "martingale" 1 hit, in census row 10 only.
findings.recommendation: Repair census row 10 so its citation matches the system it describes (either recite it to the drift-to-coherence work, or move [7] wholly into the never-run exclusion list and add the drift-to-coherence system as its own row: ML front, both timings, martingale/de Finetti coherence, downstream = multiple-choice QA accuracy, Exogenous = Yes, Sign = neutral/preserved). Add two to three sentences to §7 — best placed at the end of §7A or as a short bridge before §7B — recording the null: a training-time self-consistency loss that reduces belief drift and raises coherence while accuracy is preserved rather than improved, and the OpenForecaster case where a non-axiom-targeted RL objective raised accuracy, calibration and consistency together. The second is the best available confirmation of §7C's information-flow clause and should be cited there.

findings.location: §5A ("The enforcers") and the census table in §6A
findings.issue: A second inference-time coherence-repair operator on judge comparison graphs is absent. Prompt Perturbation for Reliable LLM Evaluation over Comparison Graphs (arXiv:2606.17634) generates perturbed variants of each prompt, uses the resulting comparison graphs to IDENTIFY AND FILTER OUT structurally inconsistent comparison patterns, and only then applies ranking aggregation — graph-level structural consistency imposed on the data before aggregation. That is an operator, not a functional, by the report's own §1A test, and it targets exactly the cyclic and tie-inconsistency patterns (A ≻ B ≻ C ≻ A; A ≡ B ≡ C ≠ A) the report treats under §5A. The report's judge-repair coverage stops at TrustJudge [2], round-robin Bradley-Terry [51] and rank fusion [52], so the judge-reliability corner the corpus populated is only two-thirds covered.
findings.evidence: Vault note `260617634-prompt-perturbation-for-reliable-llm-evaluation-over-comparison-graphs`: "we propose a prompt perturbation framework for improving the consistency of pairwise LLM evaluation. Our approach generates perturbed variants of each prompt, uses the resulting comparison graphs to identify and filter out structurally inconsistent comparison patterns, and then applies standard ranking methods to the filtered comparisons... graph-level structural consistency is incorporated explicitly into the evaluation pipeline before ranking aggregation." Adjacent uncited note `260613221-from-uncertain-judgments-to-calibrated-rankings-conformal-elo-estimati` (conformal Elo estimation; LLM-derived Elo within 17.9 MAE of human ratings over 55 held-out LMArena models) belongs to the same cluster but is measurement-only and would only qualify as contrast class. Report grep: "prompt perturbation" 0 hits.
findings.recommendation: Add one to two sentences to §5A alongside the round-robin and rank-fusion paragraphs describing prompt-perturbation graph filtering as a third inference-time judge-repair operator, and add it as a census row (ML / Inference / transitivity + tie-consistency / Formally minimal? No / downstream = leaderboard rank stability / Exogenous? Partly). If space is tight, at minimum add a clause naming it so the census's inference-time count is complete. Optionally note in §3A's measurement wave that conformal Elo estimation absorbs intransitivity statistically rather than repairing it — a useful boundary case for the measure/intervene line.

findings.location: §7E ("Two dissociation studies, and the correlational tier"), with a cross-reference in §5C
findings.issue: The corpus contains a direct, published dissociation between preference-consistency measures and downstream task effectiveness on an exogenous metric, and the report omits it while citing the same application domain positively. Position Bias Undermines Preference Consistency in Listwise LLM-Based Reranking (arXiv:2608.03091, RecSys 2026) treats rankings produced under equivalent candidate permutations as observations of an induced preference system, measures pairwise preference instability, global preference inconsistency and listwise output consistency, and finds these consistency measures "can diverge from recommendation effectiveness," with improvements in relevance failing to restore stable pairwise preferences. This is squarely the second half of the research query — the coherence/quality relationship, tested, with the answer "they come apart" — and it is on the same object (LLM ranking over an unordered candidate set) for which the report reports a POSITIVE result via LLM-RankFusion [52]. Presenting only the positive from that domain overstates the consistency-helps side.
findings.evidence: Vault note `260803091-position-bias-undermines-preference-consistency-in-listwise-llm-based`: "Experiments across multiple LLMs, datasets, and list lengths show that these consistency measures are closely aligned, but can diverge from recommendation effectiveness and marginal position-exposure bias. Improving relevance or flattening exposure across positions does not necessarily restore stable pairwise preferences, globally coherent preference structures, or consistent ranked outputs." Report grep: "reranking" 0 hits, "recommend" 0 hits; §5C's position-bias treatment rests entirely on [51].
findings.recommendation: Add two to three sentences to §7E introducing this as a third dissociation study — consistency and effectiveness measured on the same LLM rerankers and found to move independently — and add a qualifying clause to the §7A sentence about NDCG@10 gains from rank fusion [52] noting that in the same task family, consistency and recommendation effectiveness have been shown to diverge, so the rank-fusion gain should not be read as evidence that consistency drives retrieval quality. Also add a clause to §5C recording that position bias is documented to induce preference inconsistency in listwise as well as pairwise settings.

findings.location: §4C ("The Nash pole") and §5B ("The accepters, and what their numbers actually show")
findings.issue: The query names Nash learning from human feedback as one of three ML-front anchors, and the corpus supports a substantially wider Nash/von-Neumann-winner cluster than the report uses. Four on-topic notes are uncited: (a) Self-Play Preference Optimization (arXiv:2405.00675), the most widely used practical NLHF descendant, explicitly motivated by Bradley-Terry's failure on intransitive preferences; (b) S-SPPO (arXiv:2606.01561, ICML 2026), which repairs an SPPO instability rather than the intransitivity; (c) Stackelberg Learning from Human Feedback (arXiv:2512.16626), a DIFFERENT solution concept — sequential-move leader/follower rather than simultaneous-move Nash — that also yields an inference-time refinement mechanism; and (d) Asymptotic Universal Alignment (arXiv:2601.08777), which is a published CRITIQUE of the Nash pole. The report's §4C presents the Nash family entirely without internal criticism, and §4D asserts the two poles are compatible without registering that a corpus source argues NLHF's equilibrium collapses to a near-deterministic majority-preferred response. Separately, §5B's claim that "No exogenous metric appears in either paper; every downstream number is an automated-judge win rate or a preference-agreement score" is true of [12][13] but reads as a claim about the acceptance camp generally, and SPPO reports Open LLM Leaderboard results, which are not preference-judged.
findings.evidence: `240500675-self-play-preference-optimization-for-language-model-alignment`: SPPO "reaches a 28.53% length-controlled win-rate vs GPT-4-Turbo on AlpacaEval 2.0 (38.77% from the stronger Llama-3-8B-Instruct base), and outperforms iterative DPO/IPO on MT-Bench, Arena-Hard, and the Open LLM Leaderboard." `260601561-s-sppo-...`: "52.19% win rate / 47.46% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 with Llama-3-8B, accepted at ICML 2026"; described as fixing policy degeneration rather than repairing intransitivity. `251216626-stackelberg-learning-from-human-feedback-...`: "reframes preference optimization as a sequential-move (Leader/Follower) game rather than RLHF's scalar Bradley-Terry reward or NLHF's simultaneous-move Nash equilibrium... enabling inference-time refinement via iterative sampling." `260108777-asymptotic-universal-alignment-...`: popular post-training methods "INCLUDING Nash learning from human feedback fundamentally underutilize the benefits of test-time scaling... because standard alignment methods COLLAPSE to a single majority-preferred response, destroying the output diversity that test-time scaling needs"; optimal achievable rate f(k)=k/(k+1). Report grep: "self-play" 0, "SPPO" 0, "Stackelberg" 0.
findings.recommendation: Extend the existing descendants sentence in §4C (the one already listing proximal-point, multiplayer, exploratory and maximal-lottery variants) with two additions: name self-play preference optimisation and its semantic-calibration successor as the deployed instantiations of the Nash objective, and name the Stackelberg/sequential-move reformulation as a distinct solution concept in the same family that additionally supplies an inference-time refinement step. Then add one to two sentences at the end of §4C giving the pole its published critique — that the resulting equilibrium policy is often near-deterministic and collapses to a single majority-preferred response, with a proved k/(k+1) ceiling on multi-sample win rate. Finally, narrow the §5B sentence about exogenous metrics so it is scoped to the two general-preference-model papers rather than to the acceptance camp as a whole, noting that self-play NLHF descendants do report standard capability-leaderboard numbers.

findings.location: §8C ("Each side holds the corrective the other needs"), with a knock-on qualifier in §9C
findings.issue: §8C's load-bearing asymmetry claim — that machine learning "lacks a cardinal dose: it counts cycles and reports non-transitivity rates where the economics side has five graded indices" — is contradicted by an uncited corpus note. A Markov Chain Approach to Preference Alignment (arXiv:2606.22652) proves geometric convergence of an alignment procedure at a rate governed by a seminorm that literally measures the distance of the pairwise utility from a transitive (additively separable) structure, and shows via perturbation analysis that when that seminorm is small, the Markov and Nash procedures agree to first order around the RLHF solution. That is a continuous, cardinal, ML-native measure of how intransitive a preference structure is — exactly the object §8C says the field does not have, and exactly the graded dose §9C's second open cell calls for. Leaving it out makes the two-literatures asymmetry look cleaner than the corpus supports.
findings.evidence: Vault note `260622652-a-markov-chain-approach-to-preference-alignment`: "Proves MCHF converges geometrically to a stationary distribution at a rate governed by the seminorm ||U||_(+) = inf over g,f of ||U - g(+)f||_inf, which directly quantifies the non-transitive (intransitive) structure of the pairwise utility — i.e., the paper's convergence guarantee is literally parameterized by how far U is from a transitive (additively separable) structure." Adjacent uncited note `260518721-general-preference-reinforcement-learning` sits in the same family. Report grep: "Markov" and "seminorm" absent from the two-literatures section.
findings.recommendation: Qualify the §8C sentence rather than deleting it: keep the asymmetry but add a clause conceding that at least one ML-front construction does supply a continuous distance-from-transitivity parameter — a seminorm measuring how far a pairwise utility sits from an additively separable one, used as the convergence-rate constant for a Markov-chain alignment procedure — so the correct claim is that the ML front has a cardinal intransitivity measure in theory but has not used it as an experimental dose. Add a matching half-sentence to §9C's second open cell noting that the dose parameter need not be imported from economics; a native one already exists but has never been varied experimentally.

findings.location: §3A (the measurement wave) and §9C/§9D (the open cells and the proposed experiment)
findings.issue: The report's economics front assumes throughout that GARP over budget sets is a well-powered, informative test in the environments an agent experiment would use, and it builds its central recommendation on that assumption. Two corpus items say otherwise and are entirely absent. First, The Empirical Content of Revealed Preference in High Dimensions (arXiv:2605.29361) proves that under Selten's Area measure the empirical content of GARP converges to ZERO EXPONENTIALLY FAST in the number of goods, with quantitatively large effects in simulations calibrated to scanner data, and finds that available remedies slow but do not eliminate the loss. Second, the Bronars power result — the canonical statement of how likely non-maximizing behaviour is to be detected — is in the vault only as an unresolved bibliographic record, and the coverage-gaps file explicitly warns it must not be cited as read. Together these supply an alternative explanation for the report's own headline measurement fact (flagship LLM CCEI at 0.994-1.000): in a two-good, few-budget-set design the test may simply have little power, and in the high-dimensional action spaces real agents inhabit the restrictions are near-vacuous. The report gestures at this once ("a regime of limited test power that the apparatus's leading advocate concedes") and never returns to it.
findings.evidence: Vault note `260529361-the-empirical-content-of-revealed-preference-in-high-dimensions`: "While higher-dimensional choice problems may appear more demanding, we show that revealed preference restrictions become less informative. Using Selten's Area measure, we establish that for any fixed number of observations, the empirical content of GARP converges to zero exponentially fast in the number of goods... while these can slow the rate, they do not eliminate this loss of empirical content." Vault note `w1538584636` (OpenAlex record for Bronars 1987, Econometrica, 287 citations, oa_status closed, no full text anywhere). research/temp/coverage-gaps.md: "Bronars (1987) itself is `unresolved` — closed access, every route failed... Must not be cited as though read." Report grep: "high dimension" 0, "Bronars" 0.
findings.recommendation: Add two to three sentences to §3A immediately after the CCEI-above-0.997 sentence, recording that GARP's empirical content shrinks exponentially in the number of goods, so near-perfect efficiency indices in two-good agent experiments are consistent with both a highly rational agent and a near-powerless test, and that the canonical power benchmark for these tests could not be obtained in this sweep and is cited here only at second hand. Add a matching qualifier to §9D's proposed experiment: any design that scales an agent's choice environment toward realistic action-space dimension buys realism at the cost of test content, which makes the choice of dimension a first-order design parameter rather than an implementation detail. Also add a clause to §2D noting that rationalizability testing has been extended to INDIVISIBLE-object reallocation (Shapley-Scarf markets) via graph acyclicity — NP-complete in general, tractable on the single-crossing domain — since agent choice is typically over discrete options rather than divisible bundles, and the divisible-bundle framing the whole front assumes is not the only one available.

findings.issue: The philosophical/normative corner of the corpus is thinner in the report than in the vault on one specific point: indeterminacy. Preference Reasoning under Indeterminacy in Large Language Models (arXiv:2608.18631) formalises epistemic indeterminacy (incomplete or partial preferences) and structural indeterminacy (non-existence of a solution under standard social-choice concepts) and shows that state-of-the-art models systematically fail to distinguish determined from undetermined instances. This is directly relevant to the report's argument: an operator that projects onto a consistent set presupposes the projection target is non-empty and determinate, and §2C already flags the closely related well-posedness failure (the minimising set is empty for the Varian, swaps and least-squares losses). The report's treatment of incompleteness rests entirely on the shutdownable-agents result [57].
findings.evidence: Vault note `260818631-preference-reasoning-under-indeterminacy-in-large-language-models`: "real-world preference reasoning is inherently indeterminate: information may be incomplete, and valid solutions may not exist... (i) epistemic indeterminacy, arising from incomplete, partial, or expressive preferences, and (ii) structural indeterminacy, arising from the non-existence of solutions under standard social choice concepts. Across a hierarchy of tasks, we show that state-of-the-art language models systematically fail to distinguish between determined and undetermined instances." Related uncited note `260618005-llm-consumer-behavior-theory-foundations-of-a-novel-research-field` independently flags as an OPEN research question whether LLM choice consistency "can be influenced or steered... through modifications to the model itself" — third-party corroboration of the report's §9 verdict from a mid-2026 survey. Report grep: "indeterminacy" 0 hits.
findings.recommendation: Add one to two sentences to §7E beside the completeness result, noting that models fail to distinguish determinate from indeterminate preference problems, so an enforcement operator applied indiscriminately risks manufacturing a determinate answer where none exists — the behavioural counterpart of the empty-argmin problem §2C already establishes analytically. Optionally add a single clause to §9A citing the mid-2026 consumer-theory survey that independently treats intervention on LLM choice consistency as an open question, which corroborates the report's own verdict from outside its two fronts.

findings.location: Whole draft; concentrated in the executive summary, §2C, §3C, §6B, §7G, §9A and §9C
findings.issue: Content dilution. The draft runs 12,852 words / ~90KB, roughly double the 45-55KB band of the pipeline's top-performing reports. The inflation is not extra evidence; it is one thesis restated at least six times. The claim that the missing cell is 'an agent's own realised choices, perturbed minimally onto the rationalizable set, scored on an exogenous payoff' appears in the executive summary ('Nothing in the corpus takes an agent's own realised choices over budget sets, perturbs them minimally...'), at the end of §2C ('only a sketch for the object an agent experiment would want to perturb'), at the end of §3C ('only one system targets GARP, and it does so by constructing consistent data before training, not by projecting an observed choice sequence'), in §6B ('Minimal perturbation of an agent's own chosen bundles appears nowhere'), in §7G ('No published study varies choice-coherence on a fixed agent...'), and twice more in §9A and §9C. The non-identification claim is likewise stated in full in §5B, again as the whole of §7G, and again as §9B. There is also meta-narration that adds no evidence — the forward-pointer at the end of §1B, the front-separation announcement at the end of the executive summary, and the inclusion-rule preamble in §6A partly restating §1A's three grades.
findings.recommendation: Tighten in three places rather than cutting sections. (1) §7G is almost entirely a restatement of §5B's non-identification argument plus §6B's table reading; compress it to two or three sentences that add only what is new (the matched null-operator control from [4] as the single strongest causal datum) and let §9B carry the verdict. (2) Reduce the missing-cell statement to one full articulation (keep the executive summary's) and let §2C, §3C, §6B and §9A each carry a single clause pointing back to it rather than re-deriving it. (3) Delete the meta-narration: the 'The economics and machine-learning fronts are treated separately below, in §§2-3 and §§4-5' sentence, the 'One structural fact organises everything downstream, and §7 turns it into a rule' pointer, and the restatement of the functional/operator distinction inside §6A's inclusion rule. These three edits should recover 1,200-1,800 words without removing a single piece of evidence, and the space is better spent on the ELSPR, drift-to-coherence and prompt-perturbation census entries flagged above.

findings.location: Executive summary paragraph 2 vs §9B ("Half two: populated but unidentified")
findings.issue: The executive summary and the conclusion make the same argument in nearly the same words. The summary says the second half "has also been tested, repeatedly, in both directions, and every published estimate is unidentified... Reported signs disagree not because the effect is subtle but because the comparisons are confounded"; §9B says "The coherence-to-quality relationship has been measured at least eight times across seven systems, with gains and reversals both real. Every reading fails at least one of three requirements for an identified estimate... The field has many data points and no clean estimate." Same thesis, same three confounds, same closing rhetorical shape — and §7G states it a third time. This inflates length without adding value.
findings.recommendation: Differentiate the conclusion from the summary. §9B should not re-argue non-identification (the summary and §7 already did); it should state the verdict in one sentence and then spend its space on what follows for a reader who accepts it — which of the three identification failures is cheapest to fix, what a minimally sufficient design would cost, and which of the four open cells in §9C is closable with existing tooling versus which needs new theory. That is forward-looking content the executive summary does not contain and cannot duplicate.
